hook_text: Before three in the morning, thousands of workers boarded buses in KwaNdebele for a journey of hours to jobs they were not allowed to live near.
clip_script: Gold built Johannesburg. Factories built the cities bigger. The economy needed African workers. But the law said: work here, do not stay. Every African adult carried a pass book, the dompas. Without the right stamp, you could be arrested and sent away. The Group Areas Act cleared District Six and Sophiatown. Homelands pushed millions far from the cities, so huge settlements grew just across the border, and workers spent hours on buses every day. Women marched in 1956. At Sharpeville in 1960, sixty-nine people were killed. People kept coming anyway. In 1986, the pass laws fell. Today, the map of apartheid is still in every city.
visual_style: A whiteboard map of a city with a CBD, buffer zones and distant townships, a dompas stamp, and a dotted bus route from a homeland settlement to the city with a clock showing 3 am.
pacing: Steady, with a pause after Sharpeville and a firm close.
